stem: Light at a fixed frequency is incident from ordinary transparent, homogeneous, isotropic medium 1 on its locally planar interface with medium 2. The absolute refractive indices are $n_1,n_2>0$. When a propagating refracted ray exists, $i,r$ are the angles of incidence and refraction, respectively, both measured from the interface normal. Which statement gives the generally applicable refraction law?

options.text: The incident ray, refracted ray, and normal are coplanar, and $n_1\cos i=n_2\cos r$.
The incident ray, refracted ray, and normal are coplanar, and $n_1\sin i=n_2\sin r$.
The incident ray, refracted ray, and normal are coplanar, and $n_2\sin i=n_1\sin r$.
The incident ray, refracted ray, and normal are coplanar, and $n_1 i=n_2 r$, with angles in radians.

stem: At the same fixed frequency, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, $v_1,v_2$ are the phase speeds in two ordinary transparent, homogeneous, isotropic media, and $n_1,n_2$ are their respective absolute refractive indices. For light passing from medium 1 to medium 2, define $n_{21}$ as the relative index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1. Which set of relations correctly distinguishes these two types of refractive index?

options.text: $n_1=c/v_1,\quad n_2=c/v_2,\quad n_{21}=n_2=c/v_2$, independently of medium 1.

stem: Light at a fixed frequency travels from ordinary transparent, homogeneous, isotropic, nonabsorbing medium 1 toward a planar interface with medium 2, with absolute refractive indices satisfying $n_1>n_2>0$. The angle of incidence $i$ is measured from the normal, $0\le i<90^\circ$, and $i_c$ denotes the critical angle. Which statement correctly gives the critical angle and the ray behavior on its two sides?

options.text: $i_c=\arcsin(n_2/n_1)$; for $i\lt i_c$ there is a propagating refracted ray, for $i=i_c$ the refracted direction lies along the interface, and for $i\gt i_c$ total internal reflection occurs.
$i_c=\arcsin(n_1/n_2)$; for $i\lt i_c$ there is a propagating refracted ray, for $i=i_c$ the refracted direction lies along the interface, and for $i\gt i_c$ total internal reflection occurs.
$i_c=\arcsin(n_2/n_1)$; for $i\lt i_c$ total internal reflection occurs, for $i=i_c$ the refracted direction lies along the interface, and for $i\gt i_c$ there is a propagating refracted ray.
$i_c=\arccos(n_2/n_1)$; for $i\lt i_c$ there is a propagating refracted ray, for $i=i_c$ the refracted direction lies along the interface, and for $i\gt i_c$ total internal reflection occurs.

stem: In a paraxial geometrical-optics imaging model with the same homogeneous medium on both sides of the lens, $t$ denotes the separation of the two refracting surfaces along the principal axis. Which statement correctly gives the geometric condition for approximating the lens as a thin lens and its consequence?

options.text: The geometric criterion for a thin lens is that $t$ must be negligible compared with the wavelength of light; neglecting the separation of the refracting surfaces does not require comparison with curvature radii or imaging distances.
If $t$ is sufficiently small compared with the lens diameter, the effects of the two refracting surfaces can be combined into one lens plane without comparing curvature radii or imaging distances.

If $t$ is negligible compared with the refracting-surface curvature radii and the relevant object and image distances, the effects of the two refracting surfaces can be combined into one lens plane in this approximation.

If $t$ is negligible compared with the relevant object and image distances, the effects of the two refracting surfaces can always be combined into one lens plane, even when $t$ is comparable to the refracting-surface curvature radii.

stem: In the thin-lens, paraxial approximation, the same homogeneous medium is present on both sides of the lens. The incident and outgoing sides are defined by the current direction of light propagation. Which statements about the lens's principal foci are correct?

options.text: For a converging lens, rays incident parallel to the principal axis actually converge after refraction at a principal focus on the outgoing-side principal axis.
For a converging or diverging lens, rays refracted after axis-parallel incidence, or their backward extensions, all intersect at the optical center, so the optical center is the principal focus.
For a converging or diverging lens, the image of any axial object point at a finite object distance lies at the principal focus, so the principal focus is independent of object distance.
For a diverging lens, the backward extensions of rays refracted after axis-parallel incidence intersect at a virtual principal focus on the incident-side principal axis.

stem: A thin lens has the same homogeneous medium on both sides, and the paraxial approximation is used. $d$ is signed object distance, $f$ is signed image distance, and $F$ is signed focal length; all distances in this question are finite and nonzero. The convention takes real objects, real images, and real focal lengths as positive, and their virtual counterparts as negative. Which statements about the lens formula and this convention are correct?

options.text: The signed relation $\frac{1}{d}+\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{F}$ applies uniformly to real objects, virtual objects, real images, and virtual images in the stated model.
Whether the object, image, and focus are real or virtual, the magnitude-based relation $\frac{1}{|d|}+\frac{1}{|f|}=\frac{1}{|F|}$ can keep all terms positive.
For unknown image distance, write $\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{F}-\frac{1}{d}$; a positive coefficient of the $1/f$ term does not prejudge $f$ as positive.
Any point on the lens outgoing side that actually emits light there is a virtual object point under this convention, so $d<0$.
The point where an incident converging beam would meet if it were not changed by the lens is a virtual object point, with $d<0$ under this convention.

stem: In the paraxial approximation for a converging thin lens with the same homogeneous medium on both sides, light travels from left to right. The left and right principal foci lie on the incident and outgoing sides, respectively. Which incident-to-outgoing-ray rules for image construction are correct?

options.text: A ray incident parallel to the principal axis passes through the right principal focus after refraction.
A ray incident parallel to the principal axis remains parallel to the axis after refraction.
An incident ray through the left principal focus is refracted parallel to the principal axis.
An incident ray through the optical center continues along its original straight line in the thin-lens approximation.
An incident ray through the optical center is always redirected through the right principal focus after refraction.

stem: A thin lens has the same homogeneous medium on both sides, and the paraxial approximation is used. $d,f$ are the finite, nonzero signed object and image distances, respectively, with real positive and virtual negative. $H>0$ and $h\ge0$ are the magnitudes of corresponding transverse linear dimensions of the object and image, respectively, not oriented heights. Which statement correctly expresses the linear magnification $\Gamma$?

options.text: $\Gamma=H/h=|d|/|f|$; it is a nonnegative object-to-image linear-size ratio and does not indicate whether the image is upright or inverted.
$\Gamma=h/H=|f|/|d|$; it is a nonnegative image-to-object linear-size ratio and does not indicate whether the image is upright or inverted.
$\Gamma=h/H=-f/d$; it is a signed image-to-object linear-size ratio, with a negative value indicating an inverted image.
$\Gamma=(h/H)^2=(|f|/|d|)^2$; it is a nonnegative image-to-object linear-size ratio and does not indicate whether the image is upright or inverted.
